title: Composting

learn.summary: Composting turns yard and kitchen waste into the best soil amendment there is, for free. The recipe is carbon-rich browns plus nitrogen-rich greens plus moisture plus air; microbes do the rest. Finished compost is dark, crumbly, and smells like forest floor — usually 3-12 months depending on method.

do: Start a compost pile or bin this week with alternating layers of browns and greens, finishing with a browns layer on top

children.title: Browns & Greens

learn.summary: Browns are carbon (dry leaves, cardboard, straw); greens are nitrogen (grass clippings, veggie scraps, coffee grounds). Aim for roughly 2-3 parts browns to 1 part greens by volume, which lands near the ideal 25-30:1 carbon-to-nitrogen ratio. Too many greens makes a slimy stink; too many browns just sits there.

do: Stockpile a bin or bags of fall leaves or shredded cardboard next to your compost so browns are always on hand to cover greens

children.title: Hot vs Cold

learn.summary: Hot composting builds a pile at least 3x3x3 feet all at once, hits 130-150°F within days, and finishes in 1-3 months while killing most weed seeds and pathogens; it needs turning weekly. Cold composting is add-as-you-go and takes 6-12 months with no turning. Hot is faster and cleaner; cold is easier — both work.

do: Push a compost thermometer or a metal rod into your pile's center; if the rod comes out warm to hot, your pile is cooking — log the reading

children.title: Vermicomposting

learn.summary: Red wiggler worms (Eisenia fetida) eat half their body weight in food scraps daily and produce castings richer in available nutrients than regular compost. A bin kept at 55-77°F works indoors year-round — ideal for apartments. One pound of worms handles about a half pound of scraps per day.

do: Set up a worm bin from two nested plastic totes with drilled air holes, shredded-paper bedding, and one pound of red wigglers

children.title: Troubleshooting

learn.summary: Every compost problem has a boring fix. Ammonia or rotten-egg smell: too wet or too many greens — turn it and add browns. Pile not heating: too small, too dry, or nitrogen-starved — add greens and water to wrung-out-sponge moisture. Rodents: bury food scraps in the center and skip meat, dairy, and oils.

do: Grab a handful from your pile's center and squeeze: it should feel like a wrung-out sponge — add water or dry browns until it does
